summary: The deck explains the problem of over-engineering—products with excessive features, performance, complexity, and cost—and argues for frugal innovation as a response driven by affordability, value consciousness, and sustainability. It examines causes of overengineering at individual, organizational, and process levels, presents research and a Volkswagen/TUHH case study on polymer material specifications in automotive development, and includes practical design exercises on a smart water tank and a rural food delivery service.

Case Study: Over-Engineering and Frugal Innovation in Polymer Materials

The study was conducted at Volkswagen, within the department of Polymers Material Engineering, part of the broader technical development division. The organization is facing increasing challenges in developing sustainable secondary polymer materials.

A collaboration was established between Volkswagen and the Institute for Technology and Innovation Management (TIM), Hamburg University of Technology (TUHH) as a three-year action research project (starting February 2021).
The collaboration was motivated by growing interest in frugal and sufficiency-oriented innovation approaches.
Develop a method to reduce excessive performance requirements
Enable integration of sustainable material concepts
Individual Reasons: Sometimes, it's about people being too cautious or resistant to change. They might be afraid to lower specifications because they see the current high standards as 'safer’.
Company Reasons: This involves a company culture that always strives for perfection, a shared belief that they must always be 'quality-driven,' and a focus on making only the highest-quality products
Process Reasons: Lack of proper tools or methods to set different requirements for different applications. The development teams might stick to old habits
Focusing on True Needs: Instead of just copying old, high standards, engineers should look at what the product really needs to do for its specific case
Top-Down: Start from what the customer needs and then figure out the exact material requirements.
Bottom-Up: Continuously question if lower-level material requirements are more than what's actually needed for the overall system to work.
